_note: Maxims, axioms & idioms for Law.SoapBox /maxims. Legal maxims + political axioms + idioms/mottos, each with a plain gloss, provenance, and (for legal ones) the category it maps to in the legal-knowledge-graph. Facts, not verdicts: we state what a maxim MEANS and WHERE it's from, never that it is right. category ids match SEED_CATEGORIES in integrations/legal-knowledge-graph.mjs where applicable.

items.literal: Ignorance of the law excuses not
items.gloss: You are bound by the law whether or not you know it exists.
items.provenance: Roman-law maxim; standard in common-law systems.

items.term: Actus reus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea
items.literal: An act does not make one guilty unless the mind is also guilty
items.gloss: Most crimes require both a wrongful act and a guilty mental state.
items.provenance: Coke; foundational to Anglo-American criminal law.

items.literal: No one should be a judge in his own cause
items.gloss: A decision-maker must not have a personal stake in the matter — the rule against bias.
No one should be condemned unheard — the core of due process.
Courts follow prior rulings — the engine of case law.
You can only be punished under a law that existed when you acted (anti-ex-post-facto).

items.term: Ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat
items.literal: The burden of proof is on the one who asserts, not the one who denies
items.gloss: The party making a claim must prove it.
Some accidents so obviously imply negligence that the fact of them is evidence.

items.literal: The law does not concern itself with trifles
items.gloss: Courts won't act on trivial matters.
A court order requiring a jailer to justify holding a prisoner — the great writ against unlawful detention.
items.provenance: English common law; U.S. Const. art. I, §9.

items.gloss: Ask who profits — a guide to motive.

items.literal: Let justice be done though the heavens fall
items.gloss: Justice must be done regardless of consequence.

items.term: Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely
items.gloss: Concentrated, unchecked power reliably degrades those who hold it — the case for checks and balances.
items.provenance: Lord Acton, letter to Bishop Creighton, 1887.

items.term: Malo periculosam libertatem quam quietam servitutem
items.literal: I prefer dangerous liberty to peaceful servitude
items.gloss: Freedom with risk beats safe subjection.
items.provenance: Quoted by Thomas Jefferson (1787); attrib. Count Palatine.

items.literal: Let the welfare of the people be the supreme law
items.gloss: The good of the public is the highest law — invoked for the state's police power.

items.term: A little rebellion now and then is a good thing
items.gloss: Periodic dissent keeps government honest.
items.provenance: Thomas Jefferson, letter to James Madison, 1787.

items.gloss: The motto of Virginia; a declaration against tyranny. (Historically also shouted by Booth at Lincoln's assassination — stated as fact, not celebrated.)

items.term: Give me liberty, or give me death!
items.gloss: Freedom is worth dying for — a Revolutionary rallying cry.
Government may not tax those it does not represent — a founding American grievance.
Publicity as a check on state violence against protesters.

items.literal: The voice of the people is the voice of God
items.gloss: Popular will carries great authority — though it is usually quoted against its original cautionary sense.
items.provenance: Attrib. Alcuin (c. 800), who wrote it to WARN against trusting the crowd.
